jehovahs_witnesses.trinity:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that there is one God, Jehovah, the Almighty, who alone is the Creator. Jesus Christ is God's Son, whom they honor as Savior and King, but he is a separate and subordinate being, not equal to the Father. The holy spirit is God's active force, the power he uses to accomplish his will, and not a person.

For this reason Witnesses do not accept the doctrine of the Trinity. They point out that the word does not appear in the Bible and hold that the doctrine developed in later centuries, under the influence of ideas from outside Scripture. They cite Jesus' own words that the Father is greater than he is. Most other Christians regard the Trinity as central, and Witnesses know this, and they aim to show from the Bible why they read the evidence differently.
jehovahs_witnesses.father:
Jehovah's Witnesses use Jehovah as the personal name of God the Father. He is the Creator of all things and the Sovereign of the universe, and he is a loving Father to those who serve him. Jesus taught his followers to pray to the Father, and Witnesses pray to Jehovah through Jesus.

They teach that the Father is greater than the Son. The Father is the one whom Jesus calls his God, and the Father alone is Almighty. Witnesses stress the closeness of the relationship between Jehovah and those who serve him, and encourage a personal friendship with him. This differs from teaching that the Father, Son and Spirit are equal persons in one God, and Witnesses generally explain that they hold Jehovah to be the Father alone.
jehovahs_witnesses.holy_spirit:
Jehovah's Witnesses understand the holy spirit as God's active force, the power which Jehovah uses to carry out his purposes. It was used to create, to inspire the writers of the Bible, to guide and strengthen God's servants and to give them fruits such as love and joy. It is not a person, and it is not part of a Godhead.

Witnesses generally write holy spirit without capital letters, to show that they do not regard it as a person. They point to passages where the spirit is poured out, or where people are filled with it, and understand these as descriptions of a force rather than a being. Most other Christians teach that the Holy Spirit is a divine person, and Witnesses recognize this difference and explain their view from Scripture.
jehovahs_witnesses.name_of_god:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that God has a personal name, Jehovah, the common English form of the four Hebrew letters known as the Tetragrammaton. They believe that the name appears thousands of times in the Hebrew Scriptures and that Jesus made it known to his followers. Their own Bible translation uses Jehovah where the original letters appear, and in some other places.

Using and honoring the divine name is central to their faith and identity. They take the name Jehovah's Witnesses from a passage in the book of Isaiah where God calls his people his witnesses. They see making the name known as a duty and a privilege, and one of their main reasons for sharing their faith with others. Other Christians who use titles such as Lord or God for the divine name generally do not hold that using Jehovah is necessary.
jehovahs_witnesses.natures_of_christ:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus is the Son of God, and that he is a created being: the firstborn of all creation, and the one through whom Jehovah made everything else. He is mighty and honored, and is called a god in a sense that shows his high position, but he is not equal to the Almighty Jehovah.

Witnesses hold that when he came to earth he became a perfect human, and that he gave his human life as a ransom sacrifice to buy back what was lost through Adam's sin. They regard him as the only one through whom salvation comes, and as the ruling King of God's Kingdom. This differs from the traditional Christian teaching that Christ is fully God, and Witnesses know it is one of the major points on which they differ from other churches.
jehovahs_witnesses.preexistence_of_chris:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Jesus existed in heaven before he came to earth, as the first of Jehovah's creations and as his Word, the one through whom God brought other things into being. He is the only being created directly by God.

They also understand Jesus in his heavenly existence to be the archangel Michael, and they hold that Jesus is called by that name in his role as leader of the angels. This identification is based on their reading of passages in Daniel, Jude and Revelation. Other Christians who believe in the preexistence of Christ generally understand him as the eternal Son and not as an archangel, and Witnesses are used to explaining their reasoning.
jehovahs_witnesses.great_apostasy:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that after the death of the apostles the Christian church gradually fell into apostasy, as the apostles themselves had warned. In their view, false teachings such as the Trinity, the immortal soul and eternal torment in hell entered the church and true worship was lost from the earth for many centuries.

They believe that Jehovah began to restore true worship in modern times, in their understanding beginning with Bible students in the late nineteenth century, who studied the Bible and rejected teachings which they considered unbiblical. Witnesses therefore see themselves as the restored form of first-century Christianity. Most other churches do not accept the idea that true Christianity was lost, and they trace their own churches to the apostles by continuous history.
jehovahs_witnesses.heaven:
Jehovah's Witnesses believe that a limited number, 144,000, are chosen to go to heaven to reign with Christ, drawing on passages in the book of Revelation and Jesus' reference to a little flock. These are spirit-anointed Christians, and they are said to receive heavenly life after being raised from the dead.

Most Witnesses do not expect to go to heaven. Their hope is to live forever on a restored earth, and only those who have the heavenly hope share in the bread and wine at the yearly Memorial of Christ's death. Witnesses see heaven as the dwelling place of God and the angels and the place from which Christ rules. This differs from the common Christian expectation that all the faithful go to heaven, and Witnesses explain their view from the Bible.
jehovahs_witnesses.hell:
Jehovah's Witnesses do not believe in a place of eternal fiery torment. They understand the words often translated as hell, Sheol and Hades, as referring to the common grave, where the dead are unconscious. Gehenna is understood as a symbol of everlasting destruction and not of torture.

They hold that eternal conscious punishment would be contrary to the love and justice of Jehovah, and that the Bible teaches that the wages of sin is death. Those who die are not suffering, and those who are destroyed will not exist again. They see the teaching of hellfire as something that has turned many people away from God. Other Christians who believe in eternal punishment understand the same passages differently.
jehovahs_witnesses.soul_sleep:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the soul is the person, and not a separate immortal part which lives on after the body dies. When a person dies, he or she ceases to exist, and the dead are unconscious, as a passage in Ecclesiastes describes, with no knowledge of anything.

The hope for the dead is therefore the resurrection: God will remember them and bring them back to life. Witnesses find comfort in this, and see it as more realistic than an idea that the dead are already in heaven. They do not believe that the dead can hear the living, or that the living can communicate with them. This differs from teaching that the soul survives death, and Witnesses stress that the Bible presents death as a sleep from which God will awaken people.
jehovahs_witnesses.resurrection_of_the_d:
Jehovah's Witnesses look forward to a resurrection of the dead, both of the righteous and of the unrighteous, as taught in the book of Acts. Those who have been chosen for the heavenly calling are raised to spirit life in heaven, while the great majority are raised to life on earth in the coming new world.

They understand resurrection as an act of God's memory and power: Jehovah remembers those who have died, and recreates them with their identity and memories. Those raised will have the opportunity to learn about Jehovah and to serve him. Witnesses take great comfort from this hope, particularly when they lose loved ones, and they see it as the answer to death, which they regard as an enemy that Christ will finally remove.
jehovahs_witnesses.millennium:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that Christ's thousand-year reign, described in the book of Revelation, is still to come in its fullness and will follow the destruction of the present wicked system at Armageddon. During it the earth will be turned into a paradise, the dead will be resurrected and humans will be gradually raised to perfection.

They believe that Christ began to rule as King in heaven in 1914, and that his presence is invisible, with the events of the last days now taking place. At the end of the thousand years there will be a final test, and those who rebel will be destroyed. Witnesses see the millennium as a time of blessing for obedient humanity. Other Christians hold varied views about the millennium, and Witnesses distinguish theirs from those.
jehovahs_witnesses.annihilation:
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that those who persistently reject Jehovah and refuse to change will be destroyed forever, and not tormented. They read the words for everlasting punishment and destruction as meaning that the wicked cease to exist, with no hope of a future resurrection.

They believe this will begin at Armageddon, when Jehovah removes the wicked from the earth, and be completed at the final judgment at the end of Christ's rule. Witnesses stress that Jehovah takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked and wants all to repent, and that the judgment will be just. This is one of the ways in which they differ from churches that teach eternal conscious punishment, and they explain it as consistent with God's love.
jehovahs_witnesses.new_creation:
Jehovah's Witnesses believe that God's purpose is for the earth to be a paradise, and that this purpose will be carried out under the rule of Christ. They read passages from the Psalms and from the book of Revelation as promising that the meek will inherit the earth, that death and sickness will be no more, and that people will live in peace forever.

The hope is for real life on a real earth, restored to what God intended in the garden of Eden. It is not a hope of an escape from the earth to a spirit world, except for the small number with the heavenly hope. Witnesses hold that this future is close, and that it is worth sharing with others. This differs from teaching in which the final home of the redeemed is heaven, and Witnesses distinguish carefully between the two hopes.
jehovahs_witnesses.food_laws:
Jehovah's Witnesses abstain from blood, based on the commands to do so in Genesis, Leviticus and the decree of the apostles recorded in Acts. For this reason they do not eat blood, and they refuse transfusions of whole blood and its principal components: red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma.

They hold that blood represents life, which belongs to God, and that the command applies to receiving it into the body by any route. They accept other medical treatments and seek bloodless surgery and alternatives, and many fractions and procedures using their own blood are left to the individual conscience. Witnesses regard this as a matter of obedience to God and not as a rejection of medicine. Others often find this hard to understand, and Witnesses are used to explaining that it is a matter of faith.
